title: Asymmetric activation tiling and ring rate limiter — design sketch
content:
Purpose:

This is a rough design sketch for two related ideas intended to improve stable latency and throughput on multi-GPU inference fleets for variable-length workloads: (1) asymmetric activation tiling (AAT) — a per-stage tiling strategy that avoids symmetric partitioning when sequence-length distributions are skewed across a batch; and (2) ring-rate-limiter (RRL) — a soft traffic shaper for NCCL-like collectives that controls injection rate to avoid short-lived network congestion and tail latency spikes.

Context + motivation:

- We still see tail latency spikes when: (a) a small fraction of requests have much longer sequences; or (b) heterogeneous instance types (or mixed GPU memory configs) share the same NCCL rings.
- Symmetric tensor/pipeline partitioning (equal slice size across GPUs) is simple but wasteful when KV/activation occupancy is highly non-uniform across micro-batches. It leads to imbalanced all-reduce/all-gather work and sudden NCCL bandwidth bursts at stage boundaries.
- Existing mitigations (microbatching, dynamic batching, prefetched KV) help but do not fully compensate for cross-stage bandwidth contention and KV movement costs during high variance traffic.

Goals:

- Reduce 95/99th token latency by smoothing NCCL collective traffic across time and avoiding peak bursts.
- Keep average throughput within 5% of current baseline for typical pmem/seq-len distributions.
- Minimize added scheduling complexity and keep integration points clean: placement layer -> stage scheduler -> NCCL runtime extension.

Design overview:

1) Asymmetric Activation Tiling (AAT)

Idea: instead of splitting activations evenly by contiguous token ranges across GPUs, compute a per-microbatch tiling plan based on the distribution of sequence lengths within the microbatch and expected KV hits. GPUs with higher expected useful work get a larger tile; others get smaller tiles such that compute load and memory pressure are balanced.

Key pieces:
- Lightweight per-request statistics: seq_len, avg_cache_hit_ratio (from recent history), preferred_locality_hint (hot/cold key). These are pulled from the routing layer when the request enters the scheduler.
- Cost model C(gpu, tile_size) = alpha * compute(tile_size) + beta * mem(tile_size) + gamma * expected_nccl_bytes(tile_size). We keep alpha,beta,gamma tuned by offline profiling per model family.
- Tiler solves a small integer partitioning for N_gpus x tile_sizes. Real-time constraint: solver must finish in < 500us for typical microbatch sizes (<= 16). Use greedy plus one refinement iteration (local hill-climb) instead of integer programming.
- Placement invariant: tiling must keep KV affinity when possible — if a shard of KV lives on GPU_i, prefer tile ranges that produce reads hitting that shard to avoid cross-node fetches.

Behavioral example (informal):
- Microbatch of 8 requests: 6 requests seq=64, 2 requests seq=1024. Symmetric slicing (equal tokens/gpu) causes GPUs handling long sequences to dominate NCCL bytes. AAT assigns proportionally larger token slices to GPUs with more of the short requests and reduces cross-GPU activation movement for the two long requests by isolating long-range work to a subset of GPUs and allowing others to finish earlier and start serving next microbatch.

Implementation notes:
- Integration points: scheduler (compute tiling), runtime (enforce tile boundaries on kernels), KV layer (pin hot KV shards), NCCL wrapper (expose planned schedule to shaper).
- Kernel implications: some kernels assume contiguous token ranges and straightforward indexing; we must add a thin indirection (tile-offset + length) and ensure that fused-kernels understand the offset. Keep indirection in runtime only; generated kernels (XLA/Triton) can accept tile params at launch.

2) Ring Rate Limiter (RRL)

Idea: introduce a token-aware soft rate limiter that shapes the launch rate and chunk sizes of collective operations on a per-ring basis. The limiter reduces the chance of synchronous bursts from many pipelines entering the same collective at the same time.

Key pieces:
- Per-ring leaky-bucket token bucket: capacity and refill tuned to measured network capacity and acceptable injection granularity (e.g., 1MB granularity).
- Collective split policy: large all-gather/all-reduce are split into K chunks (already done in some kernels) — RRL decides chunk sizes adaptively to maintain a target bandwidth utilization window (e.g., keep average below 85% instantaneous, leaving headroom).
- Priority & preemption: interactive (low-latency) microbatches get priority tokens; background/throughput jobs are queued and fed at lower weight.
- Backpressure signals: use NIC-level queue depth (if available) and per-GPU PCIe counters as additional inputs to scale refill/slowdown.
- Soft deadlines: when a microbatch is near its latency SLO, RRL can bypass limiter for the final chunk to avoid SLO miss (fail-open behavior).

Interaction between AAT and RRL:
- AAT provides expected per-gpu NCCL bytes to the RRL per collective; RRL uses that to plan chunk counts and schedule staggers across GPUs so all contributors do not emit peak chunks simultaneously.
- For pipeline-parallel multi-stage models, scheduler coordinates stagger offsets to ensure pipeline stages inject their collectives spread across a short time window (O(100us)).

Failure modes and fallbacks:

- If tiler fails (timeout), fall back to symmetric tiling with an instrumentation event so we can correlate with performance.
- If RRL signals heavy congestion (sustained token depletion), trigger a policy: (a) reduce microbatch size proactively for that replica, or (b) redirect some requests to a fallback compatible model variant (smaller memory footprint / cheaper quantized model).

Metrics to collect (new + existing):
- per-collective bytes emitted, chunk sizes, chunk send timestamps (per GPU) -> to compute burstiness index (stddev of send rate within 10ms windows)
- tiler decisions histogram: tile_size distribution per GPU, solve latency, number of refinements
- 50/95/99 token latencies pre/post tiling, and KB of cross-GPU KV reads
- RRL token bucket fullness and refill events, bypass counts (soft-deadline overrides)
- correlation metrics: tiler timeout events -> 99p latency spikes; RRL depletion events -> increased tail.

Experiment plan (short):
- Stage 0 (offline): collect seq_len distributions for top-20 customers, profile compute/mem/NCCL bytes per model family for various tile sizes.
- Stage 1 (canary): roll AAT-only on a small dedicated cluster (8 nodes) for one popular medium-sized model (e.g., 13B family). Compare 95/99 latency and throughput vs baseline under synthetic mixed-length trace (mix: 80% short(64), 15% medium(256), 5% long(1024)).
- Stage 2: enable RRL with conservative params on canary cluster and replay traces; tune chunk_sizing policy to maintain <5% throughput loss for 95% of windows.
- Stage 3: progressive ramp to prod fleet with telemetry dashboard and auto-rollback if 99p latency increases by >10%.

Open questions / risks:
- How much extra CPU overhead will tiler add to the scheduler path? We must keep solve < 500us; if not possible, consider amortizing tiler across multiple microbatches (reuse plan) or offloading to a fast FPGA/accelerator in the future.
- Is it safe to expose per-ring shaping knobs in managed Dedicated/Private environments? Need security and audit discussion with compliance (linked: JIRA-INF-1023).
- Interaction with autoscaler: if RRL constantly throttles, autoscaler might scale up capacity unnecessarily. Need a signal from RRL to autoscaler saying "throttled_by_network" rather than raw latency.

Action items / next steps:
- Marco: prototype greedy tiler algorithm + microbench API (profiler hook) — due 2024-12-05
- Priya: NCCL-wrapper PoC that implements a simple token bucket and chunk splitter — due 2024-12-12
- Ethan: telemetry dashboard proposal & data schema for new metrics (burstiness index, tiler timeouts) — due 2024-12-08
- Sofia (owner): schedule 60m sync with infra (SRE + placement) to validate placement invariant + resource accounting — target 2024-11-12 (reschedule as necessary)

Notes / scratch ideas:
- Could we use probabilistic staggering: each contributing GPU picks a random stagger offset from an exponential distribution with mean tuned to expected RTT. Low complexity but harder to coordinate for pipeline stages.
- Consider adding a brief "warm-start" behavior where long-seq requests get isolated into a small set of GPUs and are rate-limited more aggressively at admission to avoid crowding the whole ring.

References and related threads:
- Slack: #serving-runtime thread 'nccl-latency-spikes-2024-10' (see message thread id on Confluence page)
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2145 (tiler proto types)
- JIRA: INF-1023 (RRL compliance discussion)

Appendix (toy pseudo):
- Greedy tiler sketch pseudocode:
  inputs: N_gpus, requests[ ] with seq_len and hit_ratio
  sort requests by hit_ratio descending
  initialize tiles = [0]*N_gpus
  for req in requests:
    pick gpu = argmin_{g}(tiles[g] + cost_estimate(g, req.seq_len))
    tiles[gpu] += req.seq_len
  run one pass refinement:
    for each pair (i,j): try move a small token chunk from i->j if it reduces max(tiles) and reduces expected NCCL bytes

End of sketch.

-- Sofia
